title: Describe and represent objects and the environment in terms of shape, space, time and motion

lessons.title: Shapes and objects around us
lessons.html:
Flat shapes (2-D)

Flat shapes have length and width but no thickness. You see them on plans and drawings.

  • Square – four equal sides and four square corners (right angles).
  • Rectangle – four sides, opposite sides equal, four right angles. The floor of a poultry house is usually a long rectangle.
  • Triangle – three sides. The end wall of a roof is often a triangle.
  • Circle – a round shape. Every point on the edge is the same distance from the centre. Round feeder pans and the top of a water tank are circles.

Solid shapes (3-D)

Solid objects have length, width and height.

  • Cube – like a box with all sides equal.
  • Rectangular prism (box) – like a feed store room, a brick or an egg box.
  • Cylinder – like a water tank, a feed silo body or a drum.
  • Cone – like the bottom of a feed silo, which narrows so feed can flow out.
  • Sphere – a ball. An egg is close to a sphere but stretched, called an oval shape.

Why shape matters

Shapes are chosen for a reason. A round tank is strong because water pushes evenly on all sides. A cone-shaped silo bottom lets feed slide down. Egg trays have cups shaped to hold the oval egg so it does not roll and crack. Triangles are used in roof trusses because a triangle does not bend out of shape easily.

Position words

We describe where things are using words like above, below, next to, behind, in front of, between, left and right. "The fire extinguisher is on the wall to the left of the door, below the light switch." Clear position words help others find things quickly, which is important in an emergency.

lessons.title: Measuring length, area and volume
lessons.html:
Length

Length is how long something is. We measure it in millimetres (mm), centimetres (cm), metres (m) and kilometres (km).

  • 10 mm = 1 cm
  • 100 cm = 1 m
  • 1 000 m = 1 km

Use a tape measure for buildings and fences. Hold it straight and tight and read from the zero end.

Perimeter

The perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape. A camp is 50 m long and 30 m wide. Perimeter = 50 + 30 + 50 + 30 = 160 m. You would need 160 m of fencing for one strand.

Area

Area is the amount of flat space a shape covers. It is measured in square metres (m²). For a rectangle: area = length × width.

A poultry house is 100 m long and 12 m wide. Area = 100 × 12 = 1 200 m². Farmers use floor area to plan how many birds can be kept in a house, according to the stocking density in the farm's standards and the welfare codes for the industry.

Volume and capacity

Volume is how much space a solid takes up, measured in cubic metres (m³). For a box shape: volume = length × width × height.

A water trough is 2 m long, 0,5 m wide and 0,5 m deep. Volume = 2 × 0,5 × 0,5 = 0,5 m³. One cubic metre holds 1 000 litres, so the trough holds 500 litres when full.

Capacity is how much a container can hold, in millilitres (ml) and litres (ℓ). 1 000 ml = 1 ℓ.

Mass

Mass is how heavy something is, measured in grams (g), kilograms (kg) and tonnes (t). 1 000 g = 1 kg and 1 000 kg = 1 t. A feed bag usually holds 50 kg; 20 such bags make 1 tonne.

Always write the unit with your answer. "12" means nothing; "12 m²" is clear.

lessons.title: Time and motion
lessons.html:
Telling time

Farm work runs on time: feeding times, egg collection rounds, shift changes and medication times. We use two ways of writing time.

  • 12-hour clock – uses a.m. (morning, midnight to noon) and p.m. (afternoon and night). 2 p.m. means two in the afternoon.
  • 24-hour clock – counts hours from 00:00 (midnight) to 23:59. 14:00 is 2 p.m. To change p.m. times, add 12: 7 p.m. = 19:00.

Records on farms usually use the 24-hour clock because it avoids confusion between morning and evening.

Working out time spent

A shift starts at 06:30 and ends at 15:00. From 06:30 to 14:30 is 8 hours, plus 30 minutes to 15:00, so 8 hours 30 minutes. Remember: 60 minutes = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day, 7 days = 1 week.

Calendars

A calendar shows days, weeks and months. Farms use calendars to plan: when day-old chicks arrive, when vaccinations are due, when a flock goes to the abattoir. If chicks arrive on 1 March and the plan says a task is due on day 14, count forward 14 days. Count carefully whether "day 1" is the arrival day; follow the farm's programme.

Motion and speed

Motion means moving. Speed tells how far something moves in a certain time, usually in kilometres per hour (km/h).

Speed = distance ÷ time. A bakkie drives 60 km to town in 1 hour: 60 km/h. If the distance is 30 km and you drive at 60 km/h, it takes 30 ÷ 60 = half an hour (30 minutes).

On farm roads, speed limits are set for safety: children, animals and workers walk on these roads, and dust affects houses and crops. Always drive slowly near poultry houses and stop fully at the wash bay.

Key points

  • Know common flat shapes (square, rectangle, triangle, circle) and solid shapes (box, cylinder, cone).
  • Perimeter is the distance around; area = length × width.
  • Volume of a box = length × width × height; 1 m³ = 1 000 litres.
  • The 24-hour clock runs from 00:00 to 23:59; add 12 to p.m. hours.
  • Speed = distance ÷ time.
